name: Ernest Dowson
bio: English poet of the Decadence and one of the Rhymers' Club - the loose association of young poets, meeting at the Cheshire Cheese in Fleet Street, whose two Books of the Rhymers' Club (1892, 1894) carried his work alongside Yeats, Lionel Johnson and Arthur Symons. He met Wilde in 1890 and, with Robert Sherard, visited him at Oakley Street 'in the dark days between his trials'. Living at Arques-la-Bataille near Dieppe in the summer of 1897, he was among the first friends to reach Wilde after his release, dining at Berneval on 3 June and seeing him constantly until his own return to London in mid-July; the twelve surviving letters from Wilde to him are the largest cluster of the Berneval/Dieppe months, and travel from 'Cher Monsieur le Poete' to 'Tout a toi'. Frankel calls him at this period 'one of his closest confidantes' and credits the friendship - together with Wilde's reading of A. E. Housman - as a spur to the composition of The Ballad of Reading Gaol. The correspondence resumed from Naples that October, by then largely about a debt of some 18-20 pounds Dowson owed Wilde; he died at Robert Sherard's house at Catford on 23 February 1900, nine months before Wilde, who asked Smithers to put flowers on his grave.
bio_note: Years and death date from the editors' footnotes, Complete Letters (2000), pp. 877 n. 1 ('English poet (1867-1900)') and 1173 n. 2 (died at Sherard's house at Catford, 23 February 1900). Rhymers' Club membership from p. 422 n. 2 (the Cheshire Cheese meetings, the two Books of 1892 and 1894). The 1890 meeting and the Oakley Street visit from p. 877 n. 1 (independently asserted at Sox, p. 141). The Berneval/Dieppe period from Frankel (2017), p. 113; the Ballad claim at Frankel p. 121; the Naples debt from Wilde's letters, printed pp. 957, 965, 969, 971. Also on the record: Fothergill's memoir (in Sox, p. 141) that Dowson was in love with the owner of the Café Royal but 'faithful only after his fashion'; and the editors' note (p. 1018 n. 3) that Dowson 'never married', reading the 1898 reference to a 'Mrs Dowson' as 'probably a reference to a newly acquired mistress or one of the prostitutes whose company he enjoyed'.
